web_evidence.title: Point of View in Tolkien
web_evidence.note: Christine Barkley's Mythlore article analyzes the omniscient narrator of The Silmarillion and contrasts that mode with limited third-person narration, supporting an external third-person base voice.

web_evidence.title: 'Ye Olde Authour': Tolkien's Anatomy of Tradition in The Silmarillion
web_evidence.note: Gergely Nagy's University of Szeged dissertation analyzes the unified 1977 text, its absent overt frame, and its third-person narration while distinguishing surface voice from hypothetical in-world authorship.

web_evidence.title: The Silmarillion Study Guide
web_evidence.note: The guide explicitly identifies the book's point of view as third person through an unnamed narrator and covers all constituent sections.

web_evidence.title: Death, Grief, and the Other in the Quenta Silmarillion
web_evidence.note: Structural analysis of the longest section explains that the published edition removed explicit source-narrator attributions; its dispute over omniscience concerns knowledge and bias, not a shift away from external third-person narration.

web_evidence.title: The Silmarillion by J.R.R. Tolkien
web_evidence.note: Publisher page verifies the work and its multi-era contents, but its catalog description and inaccessible scripted sample do not establish narrative person.

person_note: The controlling surface narration is third person: numerous long passages independently and externally narrate characters across the creation account, Quenta Silmarillion, Akallabêth, and the Ring history, often reporting thoughts and events no participating speaker frames. First- and second-person forms in the sample are overwhelmingly direct speech, verse, or authorial paratext. The lone narratorial 'came down to us' in q02233 is a historiographic gesture toward a receiving tradition, not sustained narration by a character participating in the events. Scholarship debates whether hidden Elven, Mannish, or compiled in-world sources underlie the published voice and whether it is omniscient, but that focalization and source question does not create a sustained first-person section. No credible evidence of alternating base person was found.
